See ''[[#Operators|Operators]]'' below for others | produced = 2007–present | number_built = 130 as of 31 January 2025{{cite web |title=Orders, Deliveries, In Operation Military aircraft by Country - Worldwide |url=https://airbus.web.factory.eu.airbus.com/sites/g/files/jlcbta136/files/2025-02/2025-01_MRS_GEN_Ord-Deliv%20by%20country.pdf |website=[[Airbus]] |access-date=20 February 2025}} }} The '''Airbus A400M Atlas'''Named after the [[Atlas (mythology)|Greek mythological figure]]. is a [[Europe]]an four-engine [[turboprop]] [[military transport aircraft]]. It was designed by [[Airbus Military]], now [[Airbus Defence and Space]], as a [[tactical airlift]]er with [[Strategic airlift|strategic]] capabilities to replace older transport aircraft such as the [[Transall C-160]] and the [[Lockheed C-130 Hercules]].{{citation |url=http://www.raf.mod.uk/equipment/a400m.cfm |title=RAF – A400m. |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090430164301/http://www.raf.mod.uk/equipment/a400m.cfm |archive-date=30 April 2009 |publisher=MOD |accessdate=15 May 2010}} The A400M is sized between the C-130 and the [[Boeing C-17 Globemaster III]]. It can carry heavier loads than the C-130 and can use [[Rough-field capability|rough landing strips]]. In addition to its transport capabilities, the A400M can perform [[aerial refueling]] and [[medical evacuation]] when fitted with appropriate equipment. The A400M's [[maiden flight]] took place on 11 December 2009 from [[Seville Airport]], Spain. Between 2009 and 2010, the A400M faced cancellation as a result of development programme delays and cost overruns; however, the customer nations chose to maintain their support for the project. A total of 174 A400M aircraft had been ordered by eight nations by July 2011. In March 2013, the A400M received [[European Aviation Safety Agency]] (EASA) certification and the first aircraft was delivered to the [[French Air and Space Force|French Air Force]] in August 2013. ==Development== ===Origins=== The project has its origins in the Future International Military Airlifter (FIMA) group, established in 1982 as a [[joint venture]] between [[Aérospatiale]], [[British Aerospace]] (BAe), [[Lockheed Corporation|Lockheed]], and [[Messerschmitt-Bölkow-Blohm]] (MBB) with the goal of developing a replacement for both the [[Lockheed C-130 Hercules|C-130 Hercules]] and [[Transall C-160]].Hewson, R. ''The Vital Guide to Military Aircraft'', 2nd ed. Airlife Press, Ltd. 2001. Varying requirements and the complications of international politics meant that progress on the initiative was slow. In 1989, Lockheed decided to withdraw from the grouping. Lockheed independently developed an upgraded Hercules, the [[Lockheed Martin C-130J Super Hercules|C-130J Super Hercules]]. With the addition of [[Alenia Aermacchi|Alenia]] of Italy and [[EADS CASA|CASA]] of Spain, the FIMA group became [[Euroflag]]. Project management evaluated twin and quad [[turbofan]] engine configurations, a quad [[propfan]] configuration, and a quad [[turboprop]] configuration, eventually settling on the turboprop option.{{Cite conference |date=3 October 2018 |title=A400M aircraft: Design requirements & conceptual definition |url=https://aulaairbus.etsiae.upm.es/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/A400M-Design-Requirements-Conceptual-Definition.pdf#page=10 |location=Madrid, Spain |pages=10–12 |given1=J.L. |surname1=López Díez |given2=J.L. |surname2=Asenjo Tornell |access-date=20 June 2020 |archive-date=19 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190919185149/https://aulaairbus.etsiae.upm.es/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/A400M-Design-Requirements-Conceptual-Definition.pdf#page=10 |url-status=dead}} Since no existing turboprop engine in the western world was powerful enough to reach the projected cruise speed of Mach 0.72, a new engine design was required. Originally, the SNECMA M138 turboprop, based on the [[Snecma M88|M88]] turbofan core, was selected, but this powerplant was found to be incapable of satisfying the requirements.{{cite magazine |title=Tracing the tangled roots |magazine= [[Flight International]] |date=9–15 November 2004 |url=http://www.flightglobal.com/FlightPDFArchive/2004/2004-09%20-%202272.PDF |page=59 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20151117231827/https://www.flightglobal.com/FlightPDFArchive/2004/2004-09%20-%202272.PDF |archive-date=17 November 2015}}{{cite magazine |title=Tracing the tangled roots |magazine= [[Flight International]] |date=9–15 November 2004 |page=60 |url= http://www.flightglobal.com/FlightPDFArchive/2004/2004-09%20-%202273.PDF |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20151118011954/https://www.flightglobal.com/FlightPDFArchive/2004/2004-09%20-%202273.PDF |archive-date=18 November 2015}}. In April 2002, Airbus Military issued a new [[request for proposal]] (RFP), which [[Pratt & Whitney Canada]] with the [[Pratt & Whitney Canada PW180|PW180]] and [[Europrop International]] answered. These nations decided to charge the [[Organisation for Joint Armament Cooperation]] (OCCAR) with the management of the acquisition of the A400M. Following the withdrawal of Italy and revision of procurement totals, the revised requirement amounted to 180 aircraft. The first flight was forecast to occur in 2008 and first delivery in 2009. In April 2005, South Africa joined the programme, with the [[Denel]] Saab Aerostructures receiving a contract for [[fuselage]] components.{{cite web |title=South Africa to Cancel its A400M Order |url=http://www.defenseindustrydaily.com/South-Africa-to-Cancel-its-A400M-Order-05919/ |publisher=Defense Industry Daily |access-date=2 May 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130520101445/http://www.defenseindustrydaily.com/South-Africa-to-Cancel-its-A400M-Order-05919/ |archive-date=20 May 2013}} Malaysia was the second country outside Europe to be involved. Malaysia through CTRM is responsible for manufacturing composite aero components for the aircraft.{{Cite web |title=Products & Services (Aerospace) |url=https://www.ctrm.com.my/ps_a400.php |url-status=live |publisher=Composites Technology Research Malaysia |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180713210623/https://www.ctrm.com.my/ps_a400.php |archive-date=13 July 2018 |access-date=13 July 2018}} The A400M is positioned as an intermediate size and range between the Lockheed C-130 and the [[Boeing C-17 Globemaster III|Boeing C-17]], carrying cargo too large or too heavy for the C-130, while able to use rough landing strips.{{Cite web |date=16 July 2010 |first=Dave |last=Harvey |title=Will the world buy the A400M? |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-10631213 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20161016055746/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-10631213 |archive-date=16 October 2016 |access-date=17 November 2016 |work=BBC News}} ===Delays and problems=== In January 2009, [[Airbus|EADS]] announced that the first delivery was postponed from 2009 until at least 2012, and indicated that it wanted to renegotiate.{{cite news |last1=Regan |first1=James |last2=Hepher |first2=Tim |title=EADS wants A400M contract change, adds delay |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/eads-idUSL915166620090109 |publisher=Reuters |date=9 January 2009 |access-date=1 July 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151018162055/http://www.reuters.com/article/2009/01/09/eads-idUSL915166620090109 |archive-date=18 October 2015}} EADS maintained the first deliveries would begin three years after the first flight. In January 2009, ''[[Financial Times Deutschland]]'' reported that the A400M was overweight by 12 tons and may not have been able to meet a key performance requirement, the ability to airlift 32 tons. Sources told ''FTD'' that it could only lift 29 tons, insufficient to carry an [[infantry fighting vehicle]] like the [[Puma (IFV)|Puma]].{{cite web |title=Airbus A400M military transport reportedly Prior tests found instability in the intended {{cvt|24|m}} hose due to [[Wingtip vortices|vortice]]s generated by the [[Spoiler (aeronautics)|spoilers]], deployed to achieve 108-130 kt air speed.{{Cite web |date=25 July 2016 |title=French aerospace laboratory details A400M refuelling tests |url=https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/french-aerospace-laboratory-details-a400m-refuelling-427792/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160726132616/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/french-aerospace-laboratory-details-a400m-refuelling-427792/ |archive-date=26 July 2016 |publisher=FlightGlobal}} In April 2016, production faults affecting 14 propeller gearboxes (PGBs) produced by Italian supplier [[Avio]] Aero were discovered. The issue, involving a [[heat treating|heat treatment]] process that weakened the ring gear, affected no other PGBs; the units involved needed changing. Airbus noted: "pending full replacement of the batch, any aircraft can continue to fly with no more than one affected propeller gearbox installed and is subject to continuing inspections." Another PGB issue involved input pinion plug cracking, which could release small metallic particles into the oil system, which is safeguarded by a magnetic sensor. Only engines 1 and 3, which have propellers that rotate to the right, were affected. The [[European Aviation Safety Agency]] (EASA) issued an Airworthiness Directive mandating immediate on-wing inspection, followed by replacement if evidence of damage was found.{{Cite news |date=5 April 2016 |title=Airbus A400M engine glitch seen taking weeks to fix |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-airbus-a400m-engines-idUSKCN0X22G7 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180623033042/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-airbus-a400m-engines-idUSKCN0X22G7 |archive-date=23 June 2018}} On 27 April 2016, Airbus warned there may be a substantial PGB repair cost.{{Cite web |date=28 April 2016 |title=Airbus Reports A400M Engine Gearbox Problems Will Cause Delays |url=http://www.defensenews.com/story/defense/air-space/2016/04/28/airbus-reports-a400m-engine-gearbox-problems-cause-delays/83643340/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=http://arquivo.pt/wayback/20160515134137/http://www.defensenews.com/story/defense/air%2Dspace/2016/04/28/airbus%2Dreports%2Da400m%2Dengine%2Dgearbox%2Dproblems%2Dcause%2Ddelays/83643340/ |archive-date=15 May 2016 |publisher=Defense News}} An interim PGB fix was certified in July 2016, greatly extending inspection intervals.{{Cite web |last=Shalal |first=Andrea |date=9 July 2016 |title=Interim fix for A400M engine issue certified: Airbus |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-airshow-britain-airbus-a400m-idUSKCN0ZP0R9 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160712100402/http://www.reuters.com/article/us-airshow-britain-airbus-a400m-idUSKCN0ZP0R9 |archive-date=12 July 2016 |website=reuters.com |publisher=Reuters}} In May 2016, Airbus confirmed that a cracking behaviour identified during quality control checks in 2011 was found in a French A400M's fuselage part. It can carry up to {{convert|37|t|ST}} over {{cvt|2000|nmi}}.{{Cite web |title=ABOUT THE ATLAS (A400M) |url=https://www.raf.mod.uk/aircraft/atlas-a400m/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190406145808/https://www.raf.mod.uk/aircraft/atlas-a400m/ |archive-date=6 April 2019 |website=RAF}} The cargo box is {{cvt|17.71|m}} long excluding ramp, {{cvt|4.00|m}} wide, and {{cvt|3.85|m}} high (or {{cvt|4.00|m}} aft of the wing). and can be configured to transport [[Air cargo|cargo]] or [[military personnel]], drop [[Paratrooper|paratroops]], conduct [[medical evacuation]]s or carry out aerial refuelling. It can operate out of short, soft landing strips and fly long-range cargo. A typical cargo load might include six Land Rovers and their trailers, or two light armoured vehicles, or a dump truck and excavator, or a [[Patriot missile system]], or a [[Aérospatiale SA 330 Puma|Puma]] or [[Eurocopter AS532 Cougar|Cougar]] helicopter, or a truck and 25-ton trailer.{{Cite magazine |date=17 February 2005 |title=Airbus builds a military airlifter: A new, multirole transporter will replace aging heavy-lift aircraft in military fleets |url=https://www.machinedesign.com/archive/article/21814411/airbus-builds-a-military-airlifter |department=Cover Story |magazine=[[Machine Design]] |volume=77 |pages=98+ |issn=0024-9114 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200624182041/https://www.machinedesign.com/archive/article/21814411/airbus-builds-a-military-airlifter |archive-date=24 June 2020 |given=Stephen J. |surname=Mraz |number=4 |url-status=live}} [[File:Airbus A400M cockpit ILA2014.jpg|thumb|Cockpit with [[side-stick]] and [[glass cockpit]] avionics]] The A400M features a [[fly-by-wire]] flight control system with sidestick controllers and [[flight envelope protection]]. Like other Airbus aircraft, it has a full [[glass cockpit]]. Most systems are loosely based on those of the A380, but modified for the military mission. The hydraulic system has dual {{cvt|20.7|MPa|psi}} channels powering the primary and secondary flight-control actuators, landing gear, wheel brakes, cargo door and optional hose-and-drogue refuelling system. As with the A380, there is no third hydraulic system. Instead, there are two electrical systems. One is a set of dual-channel electrically powered hydraulic actuators, the other an array of electrically/hydraulically powered hybrid actuators. The dissimilar redundancy provides more protection against battle damage.{{Cite web |date=10 June 2013 |title=Pilot Report Proves A400M's Capabilities |url=http://aviationweek.com/defense/pilot-report-proves-a400m-s-capabilities |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151018162055/http://aviationweek.com/defense/pilot-report-proves-a400m-s-capabilities |archive-date=18 October 2015 |publisher=Aviation Week}} In June 2019, Airbus Defence and Space was awarded a contract by the German Federal Office of Bundeswehr Equipment, Information Technology and In-Service Support (BAAINBw) to integrate and certify the J-MUSIC Directed Infrared Countermeasure (DIRCM) system into the A400M's Defensive Aids Sub-System (DASS) for the German Air Force. The DE DIRCM system, provided by Diehl Defence GmbH & Co. KG and based on [[Elbit Systems]] Ltd.'s J-MUSIC technology, enhances the aircraft's self-protection capabilities against infrared-guided missiles. The contract was scheduled to be performed over a four-year period.{{cite web |date=20 June 2019 |title=Airbus awarded contract to integrate and certify the DIRCM system |url=https://www.airbus.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2019-06-airbus-awarded-contract-to-integrate-and-certify-the-dircm-system |access-date=4 June 2025 |website=Airbus}} More than 30 percent of the airplane's structure is made of [[composite materials]]. The {{cvt|42.4|m|adj=mid}} span wing is primarily made of [[Carbon fiber reinforced plastic|carbon fibre reinforced plastic]] components, including the wing [[Spar (aeronautics)|spar]]s, the {{cvt|19|m|adj=mid}} long, {{cvt|12|–|14|mm|adj=mid}} thick wingskins, and other parts. The wing weighs about {{cvt|6500|kg|0}}, and it can carry and lift up to {{cvt|25000|kg|0}} of fuel.{{Cite magazine |year=2013 |title=A400M wing assembly: Challenge of integrating composites |url=https://www.compositesworld.com/articles/a400m-wing-assembly-challenge-of-integrating-composites |magazine=High Performance Composites |volume=21 |pages=26–31 |issn=1081-9223 |oclc=838365211 |given=Jeff |surname=Sloan |number=1}} It has an [[aspect ratio]] of 8.1, a wide chord of {{cvt|5.6|m}}, and a [[sweep angle]] of 15 degrees at 25 percent [[mean aerodynamic chord]]. The A400M has a [[T-tail]] empennage. Its vertical stabiliser is {{cvt|8.02|m}} tall. The horizontal stabiliser spans {{cvt|19.03|m}}, with a sweep of 32.5 degrees. [[File:A400M Propeller (Hamilton-Sundstrand).jpg|thumb|left|A400M [[Hamilton Sundstrand]] propeller at the [[Paris Air Show]], 2009]] The [[Ratier|Ratier-Figeac]] FH385 propellers turn counterclockwise and the FH386 clockwise.{{Cite web |title=EASA Type Certificate Data Sheet for A400M-180 |url=https://www.easa.europa.eu/sites/default/files/dfu/EASA-TCDS-A.169_Airbus_A400M-04-17072013.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180509013556/https://www.easa.europa.eu/sites/default/files/dfu/EASA-TCDS-A.169_Airbus_A400M-04-17072013.pdf |archive-date=9 May 2018 |access-date=9 May 2018 |website=europa.eu}} The eight-bladed [[scimitar propellers]] are made from a woven composite material. The aircraft is powered by four Europrop TP400-D6 engines rated at 8,250 kW (11,000 hp) each. The TP400-D6 engine is the most powerful turboprop engine in the West to enter operational use. [[File:A400M - RIAT 2013 (9360601998).jpg|thumb|A400M showing its [[counter-rotating propellers]] on each wing]] The pair of propellers on each wing [[Counter-rotating propellers|turn in opposite directions]], with the tips of the propellers advancing from above towards the midpoint between the two engines. This is in contrast to the overwhelming majority of multi-engine propeller driven aircraft where all propellers turn in the same direction. The counter-rotation is achieved by the use of a gearbox fitted to two of the engines, and only the propeller turns in the opposite direction. All four engines are identical and turn in the same direction. This eliminates the need to have two different "handed" engines on stock for the same aircraft, simplifying maintenance and supply costs. This configuration, dubbed ''down between engines'' (DBE), allows the engine to produce more lift and lessens the [[torque]] and [[prop wash]] on each wing. It also reduces [[Aircraft principal axes|yaw]] in the event of an outboard engine failure.{{Cite web |title=Focus on innovation: Down-Between-Engines (DBE) |url=http://www.a400m-countdown.com/index.php?v=2&spage=7 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080501074845/http://www.a400m-countdown.com/index.php?v=2&spage=7 |archive-date=1 May 2008 |url-status=usurped |website=[[Airbus Military]]}} Due to these benefits, the vertical stabiliser can be reduced by 17 percent in size, while the size of the horizontal stabiliser can be shrunk by 8 percent.{{Cite news |date=9–15 November 2004 |title=Under the skin: Airbus Military's airlifter has several things in common with its commercial siblings, sharing dimensions and composites technology that were pioneered for airliners |volume=166 |pages=46+ |work=[[Flight International]] |issue=4959 |department=A400M: Airframe |location=Toulouse, France |url=https://www.flightglobal.com/under-the-skin/57584.article |url-status=live |url-access=limited |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200702194536/https://www.flightglobal.com/power-demands/67488.article |archive-date=2 July 2020 |issn=0015-3710 |given=Guy |surname=Norris}} A [[forward-looking infrared]] enhanced vision system (EVS) camera provides an enhanced terrain view in low-visibility conditions. The EVS imagery is displayed on the [[Head-up display|HUD]] for low-altitude flying, demonstrating its value for flying tactical missions at night or in clouds. EADS and Thales provide the new Multi-Colour Infrared Alerting Sensor (MIRAS) missile warning sensor for the A400M.{{cite web |title=IR Sensors Page 4 English Seite 5 deutsch |url=http://www.iaf.fraunhofer.de/pdf/jahresbericht-2006/sensor.pdf |publisher=[[Fraunhofer Society|IAF.Fraunhofer]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090731042619/http://www.iaf.fraunhofer.de/pdf/jahresbericht-2006/sensor.pdf |archive-date=31 July 2009}}{{cite web |title=EADS and Thales to supply latest-technology missile warner to A400M |url=http://www.globalsecurity.org/military/library/news/2005/09/mil-050928-eads01.htm |website=globalsecurity.org |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060107202706/http://www.globalsecurity.org/military/library/news/2005/09/mil-050928-eads01.htm |archive-date=7 January 2006}} The A400M has a removable refuelling probe mounted above the cockpit, allowing it to receive fuel from drogue-equipped tankers.{{Cite web |title=Military Aircraft Airbus DS – A400M |url=http://www.airbusmilitary.com/Aircraft/A400M/A400MAbout.aspx |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140701075336/http://www.airbusmilitary.com/Aircraft/A400M/A400MAbout.aspx |archive-date=1 July 2014 |access-date=9 May 2015 |website=[[Airbus Military]]}} Optionally, the receiving probe can be replaced with a fuselage-mounted UARRSI receptacle for receiving fuel from boom equipped tankers.{{Cite web |title=A400M as a tanker |url=http://www.c295.ca/wp-content/uploads/a400m-tanker-data-sheet.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923195621/http://www.c295.ca/wp-content/uploads/a400m-tanker-data-sheet.pdf |archive-date=23 September 2015 |access-date=14 May 2013 |website=[[Airbus Military]]}} The aircraft can act as a tanker when fitted with two wing mounted hose and drogue under-wing refuelling pods or a centre-line Hose and Drum unit. The refuelling pods can transfer fuel to other aircraft at a rate of {{cvt|2640|lb/min|order=flip}}. The team was sent to treat a British national with suspected [[hantavirus]]; he was a local island resident who disembarked from the virus-hit cruise ship [[MV Hondius]]. Oxygen supplies at the island's hospital had reached a critical level. The territory normally operates with just a two-person medical team. Six paratroopers and two military clinicians from the [[16 Air Assault Brigade]] launched the mission. Because of the specialised medical care required, an intensive care nurse and an intensive care doctor were strapped to paratroopers for tandem jumps. The team flew 6,788 km from [[RAF Brize Norton]] to [[Ascension Island]]. They then flew over 3,000 km to the drop zone, supported by mid-air refuelling from an RAF [[Airbus A330 MRTT|Voyager]]. Medics battled winds exceeding 25 mph to land safely on the island's rocky golf course. Once airborne, the crew contacted air traffic controllers just before the crash about a technical failure,{{Cite news |last=Alexander |first=Harriet |date=9 May 2015 |title=Video: Military plane crashes during test flight near Seville |work=Telegraph |location=London |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/europe/spain/11594603/Military-plane-crashes-during-test-flight-near-Seville.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180624032908/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/europe/spain/11594603/Military-plane-crashes-during-test-flight-near-Seville.html |archive-date=24 June 2018}} before colliding with an electricity pylon while attempting an emergency landing.{{Cite web |author=Teresa López Pavón |date=9 May 2015 |title=Cuatro muertos tras estrellarse un avión militar A-400M en pruebas junto al aeropuerto de Sevilla |url=http://www.elmundo.es/andalucia/2015/05/09/554df2d6ca4741bd328b456e.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150509200737/http://www.elmundo.es/andalucia/2015/05/09/554df2d6ca4741bd328b456e.html |archive-date=9 May 2015 |website=ELMUNDO |language=es}} The crash was attributed to the [[FADEC]] system being unable to read engine sensors properly due to an accidental file-wipe, resulting in three of its four engines remaining in "idle" mode during takeoff.{{Cite news |title=Fatal A400M crash linked to data-wipe mistake |work=BBC News |date=10 June 2015 |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-33078767 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150610200925/http://www.bbc.com/news/technology-33078767 |archive-date=10 June 2015 |access-date=10 June 2015}} ==Controversies== ===Export Control breaches=== In July 2026, Airbus announced that it had paid a fine of £6.4 million to UK revenue and ‌customs authorities to settle a two-year-old investigation into export control violations. The investigation focused on anomalies over the cross-border transfer of parts for the A400M military airlifter that came to light during an audit in 2022.{{Cite web|url=https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/airbus-says-it-paid-6-million-fine-uk-export-control-probe-2026-07-29/|title=Airbus says it paid £6 million fine in UK export control probe|work=Reuters|access-date=30 July 2026}} According to HMRC sources, the breaches included:{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/jul/30/airbus-fined-64m-hmrc-export-technology-breaches|title=HMRC fines Airbus £6.4m for breaching rules on export of sensitive technology|work=The Guardian|access-date=30 July 2026}} * Failing to keep accurate records of transfers of controlled technology as per the conditions of three of their open general export licences (OGELs) * Failing to keep registers in relation to OGELs * Failing to keep accurate records contrary to the conditions of one of their OGELs * A failure of licence conditions on a standard individual export licence (SIEL)
